title: Electronics — Chapter 7: The PCB Design Stackup

questions.question: In Chapter 7, “stack-up” refers to:
options: Only the cardboard box used to ship bare boards.
The composition and layering order of materials used in PCB lamination.
The order of emails sent to CAM during a disposition loop.
The sequence of quote revisions sent during a disposition loop.
questions.explanation: composition and layering order of the materials used in lamination

reference.book: The Hitchhiker's Guide to PCB Design
reference.excerpt: From Two to More The term “stack-up” refers to the composition and layering order of the materials used in lamination of the PCB.

books.excerpt: Rogers is not suitable for sequential lamination process, and there are other material vendors, like Taconic and Isola, who make materials that perform similar to Rogers and do not have these limitations.

questions.question: A sound stack-up strategy matters because layer positions affect:
options: Only the PDF thumbnail color in the file browser.
Electrical performance and manufacturing/cost realities of the board.
Nothing if the schematic used IEEE reference designators.
Only the silk-screen font licensed by marketing.
questions.explanation: will not only affect the PCB’s electrical performance

reference.book: The Hitchhiker's Guide to PCB Design
reference.excerpt: Click to Enlarge Selecting a sound PCB stack-up strategy is important because where the etched and plated layers are positioned and laminated from topto-bottom will not only affect the PCB’s electrical performance, but its mechanical performance as well.

questions.question: When documenting impedance in the stack-up detail, designers should:
options: Invent dielectric constants so fabs cannot change anything.
Validate impedance line widths in the stack-up and let suppliers adjust process variables carefully.
Omit reference planes so impedance becomes a surprise at ICT.
Set every layer to one mil dielectric by software default.
questions.explanation: validate the values in the stack-up

reference.book: The Hitchhiker's Guide to PCB Design
reference.excerpt: For controlled impedance, adopting a stack-up philosophy which allows the board supplier to vary the dielectric constant of materials, trace widths, and spacing to achieve the specified impedance is recommended.

questions.question: High-Speed guide — a typical tolerance on final impedance is about:
options: ±50%, which is always acceptable for USB and DDR alike.
±10% typical (some fabs advertise tighter, e.g. ±5%).
Exactly 0% because copper never varies in production.
±100%, so controlled impedance notes are decorative only.
questions.explanation: A typical tolerance on the final impedance is +/- 10%

reference.excerpt: A typical tolerance on the final impedance is +/- 10%. But Sierra Circuits is capable of achieving +/- 5% impedance tolerance.

questions.question: Controlled dielectric stack-up (High-Speed) focuses manufacturing on:
options: Ignoring materials entirely and only checking silk-screen.
Building the specified dielectric construction when impedance traces are not the control method.
Deleting all ground planes to save laminate cost.
Using only air as the dielectric between every copper layer.
questions.explanation: The designer provides the controlled dielectric stack-up

reference.excerpt: Since impedance traces are not specified here, the manufacturing focus is completely upon building a board within +/- 10% tolerance of the specified dielectric thickness from layer to layer.

questions.question: Adding ground/power planes when moving beyond two layers is described as:
options: Free in every fab quote with no cost impact ever.
A common multi-layer choice that increases cost versus a simple two-layer board.
Illegal under ITAR for all commercial products.
Only useful for making the board thicker for shipping weight.
questions.explanation: average cost of adding a layer

reference.book: The Hitchhiker's Guide to PCB Design
reference.excerpt: Power planes are simply formed by adding layers of copper foil to the stack-up and connecting them to power or ground.

books.excerpt: The routing is then completed. 7.3.1 Best Routing Practices for High-Speed Routing 7.3.1.1 Ground and Power Planes One of the most usual problems in PCB design, and also in the system design, is the lack of a good ground structure.

reference.book: The Hitchhiker's Guide to PCB Design

questions.question: SpaceX avionics sourcing angle on stack-up:
options: Buyers never need to read stack-ups if piece price looks low.
Reading stack-ups/fab notes is required literacy for guiding suppliers and DFM trades.
Stack-up is only a mechanical drawing title block field.
Any stack-up works if the online fab rating is above four stars.
